patent: Filed 1989-11-27 and issued 1991-04-02 to Emmanuel Desurvire, Clinton R. Giles, Jay R. Simpson and John L. Zyskind, assigned to AT&T Bell Laboratories. The erbium-doped fiber amplifier (EDFA) had been demonstrated in 1987 by R. J. Mears, L. Reekie, I. M. Jauncey and D. N. Payne at the University of Southampton (Electronics Letters, 1987) and by E. Desurvire, J. R. Simpson and P. C. Becker at Bell Labs (Optics Letters 12(11), 1987, cited on the front page). Erbium amplifies near 1.53 to 1.56 μm, the low-loss window of silica fiber, but as a three-level system any ion that is not strongly pumped absorbs the signal. The patent's design rule, claimed as a pump mode whose radius exceeds the radius of the erbium distribution, is to confine the dopant to the high-intensity center of the pump mode with a small, high-index-difference core (1.81 μm radius, NA 0.23, pump mode radius about 3 μm). It reports 37 dB gain, 11.3 dBm output saturation power and 2.1 dB/mW gain coefficient at a 1.49 μm pump, measured with a color-center laser standing in for the 1.48 μm laser diodes then emerging. It also teaches aluminum co-doping of the core. Small-core, high-NA erbium fiber, usually Al co-doped and diode-pumped at 980 nm or 1480 nm, became the standard optical amplifier of long-haul, submarine and wavelength-division-multiplexed systems in the 1990s.

figs.1: Generic four-level scheme. The wavy arrow is pump absorption from E_{1} to E_{4}; the dashed arrow is fast non-radiative decay to the upper laser level E_{3}; the straight arrow E_{3} to E_{2} is the amplified signal transition; the lower laser level E_{2} then empties quickly to the ground state E_{1}, so it stays nearly unpopulated. Level lines are drawn dashed where only the pump arrow crosses them.
figs.2: Three-level scheme of erbium: pump from E_{1} to E_{3}, fast decay to E_{2}, and the signal transition ends on the ground state E_{1} itself. Because the lower laser level is the ground state, gain in this idealized scheme needs more than half the ions excited, and ions that the pump does not reach absorb at the signal wavelength.
figs.3: Prior-art fiber, drawn as a refractive-index profile across a diameter with the pump-mode intensity overlaid. The tall rectangle is the doped core 50 and the low flat lines either side are the cladding 52, with the mode's tails drawn just above them; the bell curve 54 is the pump mode, narrower than the core. The short vertical tick marks the fiber axis. Dots 62 and 64 near the axis sit in strong pump light; dots 56, 58 and 60 near the core edge see little pump and, per the text, mainly absorb signal.
figs.4: Laboratory test bench, drawn as a free-space optical layout. Pump path (top): color-center laser 10, a turning mirror, grating 12, then polarizing beam splitter 22. Signal path (bottom): laser diode 14 (the bracket spans its external-cavity grating, two lenses and the diode, whose outward arrows mark emission), a lens, polarization-controller loops 20, a lens, a mirror and isolator 16, then up into 22. The combined beam is lens-coupled into lead 34 of fused coupler 28; the through port is spliced at 26 to the erbium fiber coil 24, whose angled end 30 exits through a lens, a mirror and filter 35 to a beam splitter that sends light to the spectrometer (dashed) or through an unlabeled box to a detector. The coupler's 1% port 32 feeds the power-monitor detector; the fourth lead dips into oil 29. Circles with inward arrows are photodetectors; unnumbered ellipses are lenses and hatched lines mirrors.
figs.5: Signal gain versus launched pump power for the 47.5 m fiber: squares are measurements, the solid line a curve drawn through them. Gain crosses 0 dB near 6.5 mW and approaches 37 dB near 54 mW. The text derives its 2.1 dB/mW gain coefficient from +25.2 dB at 11.3 mW; the plotted squares read about 21 dB near 11 mW and 25 dB near 14 mW. The inset is the output spectrum on a logarithmic scale (A.U. in dB) against wavelength in micrometres (the axis label prints '(λm)'): the left peak, clipped at the top, is residual pump near 1.493 μm; the narrow peak is the amplified signal at 1.531 μm, on the broad amplified-spontaneous-emission band reaching about 1.575 μm.
figs.6: The patent's fiber, drawn as in FIG. 3: index step 36 for the doped core, cladding 38, and pump mode 42 now wider than the core, with much of its power in the cladding. The whole doped core lies under the upper part of the mode, so every erbium ion sees a high pump intensity. The CLAD / CORE / CLAD dimension arrows mark the core width.
figs.7: Input and output saturation powers, defined in the text at 3 dB gain compression, versus launched pump power; squares are measurements at four pump levels and lines are curves drawn through them. Output saturation power rises with pump power to about +11 dBm, as expected for a three-level amplifier, while input saturation power falls because small-signal gain rises. The description's reference to 'FIG. 4' for the range of output saturation powers evidently means this figure.

parts.14: The bracket spans the whole signal source: the grating that closes the external cavity, two lenses and the diode between them.
parts.18: The text calls this a fiber pig-tail '(not shown)' placed between controller 20 and isolator 16; in FIG. 4 the numeral points to the beam between the turning mirror and isolator 16.
parts.20: Drawn as fiber loops; loop-type controllers change polarization by bend-induced birefringence as the loops are rotated.
parts.24: The core radius is 1.81 μm, NA 0.23 and Er^{3+} concentration 2×10^{24} m^{-3} (about 50 ppm Er_{2}O_{3}); the fiber used for FIG. 5 is 47.5 m long.
parts.26: Not named as a noun; the text says amplifier 24 'is butt-spliced at 26' to the straight-through output fiber of coupler 28, so 26 marks that butt splice.
parts.28: Coupling coefficient 0.012, so nearly all combined pump and signal light goes to the through port and about 1% to port 32.
parts.29: Holds the unused input-side lead of the coupler (the text's 'other end of the monitor lead'), so that this end reflects no light back into the setup.
parts.30: Polished at ten degrees so that the end-face reflection is not guided back into the amplifier.
parts.34: Also polished at ten degrees to prevent feedback.
parts.35: 2.6 nm FWHM, centered at 1.531 μm, passing the signal and blocking pump and most amplified spontaneous emission.

glossary.def: Silica fiber whose core contains Er^{3+} ions; pumped light inverts the ions, and a signal near 1.53 to 1.56 μm passing through is amplified by stimulated emission without leaving the fiber.

In a four-level laser medium the lower laser level lies above the ground state and empties quickly, so little pumping gives gain. In a three-level medium the lower laser level is the ground state, so more than half the ions must be excited before there is gain.

The 1.53 μm transition runs from the ^{4}I_{13/2} manifold to the ^{4}I_{15/2} ground manifold. A 1.48 to 1.49 μm pump excites ions into the top of ^{4}I_{13/2} itself; a 980 nm pump excites ^{4}I_{11/2}, which decays to ^{4}I_{13/2}.
The set of closely spaced sublevels into which the host glass's electric field splits each rare-earth energy level; broadening at room temperature blurs them into a band.
More ions in the upper laser level than in the lower one, the condition for net stimulated emission.
The pump power at which the fiber's signal gain is exactly 0 dB: absorption by unexcited ions just balances emission by excited ones.
Here, the local pump power needed to invert the medium at a point in the fiber; transparency of a long fiber needs several times this at the input because the pump is absorbed along the length.
Small-signal gain in dB divided by launched pump power in mW, quoted at its maximum (the tangent from the origin to the gain curve); a figure of merit for pump efficiency.
The input or output signal power at which gain has dropped by a set amount (here 3 dB) from its small-signal value.
Power in decibels relative to 1 mW: 0 dBm = 1 mW, +11 dBm is about 12.6 mW, -20 dBm = 10 μW.
Spontaneously emitted photons amplified along the fiber; the broad background in the FIG. 5 inset and the main noise source of the amplifier.
The radius ω of the guided mode, which the patent takes at 1/e of peak intensity (the usual mode-field radius is taken at 1/e^{2}).
The sine of the acceptance half-angle of a fiber, set by the core-cladding index difference; a higher NA allows a smaller core and a tighter mode.
Core index minus cladding index; the patent quotes values from 0.019 to 0.04.
How much of the mode's intensity falls on a region, here the doped core or the other fiber's mode; it sets both pumping efficiency and splice loss.
A tunable near-infrared laser using an alkali-halide crystal (here NaCl:OH) with optically active lattice defects, itself pumped by another laser; its 1.064 μm pump light is what grating 12 removes.
A magneto-optic device that passes light in one direction and blocks it in the other, protecting a laser from back-reflections.
A cube that transmits one linear polarization and reflects the orthogonal one; here it merges orthogonally polarized pump and signal beams into one path.
Two fibers twisted and fused side by side so that light transfers between their cores by a set ratio.
A joint in which two cleaved fiber ends are aligned end to end.
A short length of fiber attached to a component as its optical input or output.
A liquid with nearly the refractive index of glass; a fiber end immersed in it reflects almost no light.
Resonances from light bouncing between two reflecting surfaces, which ripple the gain and can make an amplifier oscillate.
Full width at half maximum, the width of a spectral peak at half its peak height.
A semiconductor laser chip with anti-reflection-coated facets used as a single-pass amplifier, the main competing optical amplifier in the late 1980s.
